title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In fabless semiconductors, you own the architecture and the gross margin—until a memory or packaging bottleneck forces you to put $390 billion of purchase commitments on the table.
epigraph.author: Semiconductor Supply Chain Forensics

web_blocks.html: NVIDIA operates a fabless manufacturing model [8, 9]. It designs silicon, systems, and software in-house, while outsourcing wafers, packaging, and memory to concentrated Asian partners [8, 9]. TSMC fabricates Rubin GPUs on its N3 (3nm) node and Vera CPUs on advanced nodes [12]. It assembles multi-die packages using CoWoS-L (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate with Local Silicon Interconnect) [12]. SK Hynix and Micron supply High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM3e for Blackwell, HBM4 for Vera Rubin) [9, 12]. ODMs and OEMs like Foxconn, Quanta, Dell, Supermicro, and HPE integrate HGX boards and NVL72 liquid-cooled racks for end buyers [9, 12].

This capital-light model yields extraordinary P&L unit economics. However, it now requires massive off-balance-sheet supply commitments to lock in capacity. In FY2026, NVIDIA generated $215.94 billion in revenue with only $6.04 billion in CapEx (2.8% of revenue) [4, 11]. It converted 44.8% of revenue ($96.68 billion) into free cash flow [4, 11]. In Q3 FY27, total supply and capacity commitments jumped sequentially from $279 billion to ~$390 billion [8, 9]. Roughly $69 billion is due in the rest of FY27, and ~$203 billion is due in FY28 [8, 9]. Management noted that multi-year HBM memory procurement drove most of this surge [9]. Rising memory prices and the Vera Rubin ramp will compress Q4 FY27 gross margins to a guided 71.0%–72.0% trough [2, 9]. That marks a ~340 bps drop from 74.8% in Q3 FY27, before an expected rebound toward 72%–73% in FY28 [2, 9].

web_blocks.caption: NVIDIA FY2026 Audited GAAP P&L-to-FCF Waterfall ($ Billions, per FY2026 Form 10-K)
web_blocks.takeaway: On $215.94B of revenue ($215,938M), NVIDIA incurred $62.48B COGS ($62,475M) for $153.46B gross profit (71.1% GAAP GM). Total OpEx of $23.08B ($18.50B R&D + $4.58B SG&A) includes $2.84B D&A ($2,843M) and $6.39B SBC, leaving $130.39B GAAP operating income (60.4% margin). After $0.26B interest expense, $11.32B interest & other income (including $2.30B interest income and equity investment gains), and $21.38B tax (15.1% effective rate), GAAP net income reached $120.07B ($120,067M). Operating cash flow was $102.72B ($102,718M) and CapEx was $6.04B ($6,042M), yielding $96.68B Free Cash Flow. NVIDIA does not break out payroll separately in its GAAP 10-K income statement, so compensation for its 42,000 employees is embedded inside COGS, R&D ($18.50B), and SG&A ($4.58B).

web_blocks.takeaway: NVIDIA's fabless CapEx is tiny ($6.04B in FY26), but its balance sheet now carries $390B in off-balance-sheet supply commitments—creating operating leverage on the upside and severe write-down risk if demand ever pauses.

web_blocks.title: The $390 Billion Supply Commitment Paradox
paragraphs: In Q3 FY27, NVIDIA's supply commitments reached ~$390 billion—more than 1.8x its entire FY2026 revenue [8, 9]. Roughly $203 billion of those commitments come due in FY28 [8, 9]. These contracts lock SK Hynix, Micron, and TSMC into NVIDIA's roadmap and starve rivals of HBM4. Yet they also shift a variable-cost fabless model into a high-fixed-commitment structure if hyperscaler capex slows.

book_paragraphs: To see why NVIDIA's income statement looks like a software company's while its supply chain behaves like a heavy industrial utility, you and I should walk down the FY2026 cash waterfall line by line. On $215.94 billion of revenue, NVIDIA paid $62.48 billion for wafers, memory, and assembly—leaving $153.46 billion of gross profit, a 71.1% GAAP gross margin. Operating expenses were remarkably lean: $18.50 billion for R&D and just $4.58 billion for SG&A, which together include $2.84 billion of depreciation and amortization. Notably, NVIDIA does not break out payroll separately in its GAAP 10-K income statement, so employee compensation for its 42,000 employees is embedded inside COGS, R&D ($18.50B), and SG&A ($4.58B). That left $130.39 billion of GAAP operating income—a 60.4% operating margin.

Below the operating line, NVIDIA paid a negligible $259 million in interest, earned $11.32 billion in interest and investment gains, and paid $21.38 billion in taxes (a 15.1% effective rate), delivering $120.07 billion in GAAP net income. Operating cash flow hit $102.72 billion, and because TSMC and SK Hynix own the fabs, NVIDIA spent only $6.04 billion on CapEx—leaving $96.68 billion in free cash flow.

Yet there is a hidden catch in that fabless miracle, and it just jumped off the page in Q3 FY27. To guarantee enough TSMC CoWoS-L packaging and SK Hynix HBM4 memory for Vera Rubin, NVIDIA expanded its multi-year supply and capacity commitments from $279 billion in Q2 FY27 to roughly $390 billion in Q3 FY27—with $203 billion coming due in fiscal 2028 alone.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The $390 billion supply commitment is a double-edged sword. In a supply-constrained AI boom, it acts as a competitive weapon that locks up HBM4 and CoWoS capacity. In a sudden demand air-pocket—like the 2025 H20 export ban that forced a $4.5 billion write-off—those commitments turn into instant inventory liabilities.

book_subsections.title: Why Gross Margins Dip to 71%–72% in Q4 FY27
paragraphs: Interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress gave us a candid look at unit-cost friction on the Q3 FY27 call. While Q3 gross margin held at 74.8%, management guided Q4 FY27 down to 71.0%–72.0%, calling it the expected trough of the product cycle. Two forces are squeezing those 340 basis points: first, the initial manufacturing ramp of Vera Rubin NVL72 racks carries lower early yields; second, HBM4 memory prices are rising sharply, and NVIDIA absorbed part of that inflation while honoring pre-existing customer purchase orders.

Meanwhile, channel concentration remains high: two direct customers—Customer A at 22% and Customer B at 14%—accounted for 36% of FY2026 revenue, and U.S. export rules have effectively zeroed out Data Center compute shipments to China. Keeping gross margins above 71% despite rising memory costs and zero China volume is a testament to pricing power, but you and I should watch whether FY28 margins actually rebound to 72%–73% as promised.

book_subsections.title: Inside the Fabless Bottlenecks: TSMC CoWoS-L & HBM4
paragraphs: To understand why NVIDIA had to lock up $390 billion in supply commitments—including $203 billion due in FY28—you have to look at the physical bottlenecks inside a Vera Rubin NVL72 rack. Each Rubin GPU packs roughly 336 billion transistors across dual reticle-sized compute dies built on TSMC's N3 (3nm) process, stitched together on TSMC's CoWoS-L interposer alongside eight stacks of HBM4 memory totaling 288 GB per GPU (20.7 TB per rack) at 22 TB/s of bandwidth.

Only three companies on earth—SK Hynix, Micron, and Samsung—can supply leading-edge HBM at scale, and SK Hynix captures the largest share of NVIDIA's memory spend. By signing multi-year take-or-pay and capacity reservations with SK Hynix, Micron, and TSMC, NVIDIA effectively pre-buys the industry's scarce packaging and memory capacity. That starves competing merchant GPUs and custom ASICs of supply during an upswing, while shifting fixed-commitment risk onto NVIDIA's shoulders if AI infrastructure spending ever pauses.
